hey my ac unit outside is making this weird humming noise but the fan isnt actually spinning. is there something wrong with it? also what should i look out for before i go poking around it?

A humming noise with a non-spinning fan is a classic sign of a failing capacitor, which gives the motor its initial kick to start spinning. It could also be a seized motor bearing or a wiring issue. Before you poke around, make sure the unit is completely powered off at the thermostat and the breaker panel—that's non-negotiable. Also, check for any visible bulging or leaking on the capacitor (it looks like a small metal cylinder), and be aware that it can hold a dangerous electrical charge even when unplugged, so discharge it with an insulated screwdriver if you're comfortable. And if you see any burnt wires or smell something like ozone, stop and call a pro. Honestly, a capacitor swap is a cheap fix, but a seized motor means a bigger job. I'd say it's a 50/50 chance it's the capacitor, but if you're not handy with electrical parts, it's worth a service call. Just remember: the fan not spinning is the symptom, not the problem—it's the motor's "stuck in the mud" moment.

ok so i checked the breaker and turned it off. i saw the capacitor and it looks a bit swollen on top like it's bloated or something. i dont really want to mess with the wires myself though. is that swelling a definite sign it's blown? and is there anything else that could cause that humming sound if it wasnt the capacitor?

A swollen, bloated capacitor is a very strong sign it's failed—that bulging top is the internal pressure from a shorted or overheated dielectric, and it's essentially a dead component. It's not a "definite" 100% guarantee, but it's about as close as you get without a multimeter. If it's swollen, it's done, and it needs replacing. Since you don't want to mess with the wires, that's the right call—a capacitor can hold a nasty charge, and a pro will discharge it safely and swap it in minutes. 

As for other causes of the hum with a stuck fan: a seized motor bearing (the shaft won't turn by hand even with power off) is the other big one, or a bad contactor/relay that's sending power but not engaging properly. A failing run capacitor is the most common culprit, but a motor that's just worn out can also hum and refuse to spin. If the capacitor is swollen, though, that's your smoking gun—the motor is likely fine, and the cap is just refusing to give it that starting jolt.

it's kinda spooky how it just makes that sound out of nowhere. like it's almost intentional or something. do you think there's any chance it's just some weird electrical glitch or something like that?

It can definitely feel spooky, but it's not intentional—it's just physics doing its thing. The hum is the motor straining against the locked rotor, and the swollen cap is the physical proof that it's not a glitch; it's a component that gave up. Electrical "glitches" are usually more like flickering lights or random resets, not a steady hum with a visibly deformed part. That swelling is a hard, mechanical failure, not a ghost in the machine. 

Think of it like a stubborn old mule—it's not being dramatic, it's just stuck. The capacitor is the one that's supposed to give the motor a kick in the rear to get moving, and it's too bloated to do its job. So no, it's not a glitch; it's a worn-out part that needs a replacement. 

If you're feeling uneasy about it, that's your gut telling you to leave it to a pro—which is exactly the right instinct. A technician will have it humming (the good kind) in no time. And hey, at least it's not a swarm of angry hornets in there—that would be a whole different kind of spooky.
